result: Prior work has established that perceptual decision making typically involves accumulation of sensory information, with advantages to knowing when evidence will appear. Mistiming accumulation onset can lead to errors, and mechanisms for controlling accumulation onset timing include both sensory-driven triggers and top-down control based on temporal context.
evaluation: Claims C1-C9 are all literature review claims supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These establish the background context for the current study and are well-documented in the cited literature.

result: The CPP and Mu/Beta signals are established neural markers of evidence accumulation and motor preparation. The CPP builds gradually at a rate proportional to evidence strength, peaks at response, predicts accuracy and RT, and encodes cumulative evidence. Motor signals show distinct strategic adjustments including stereotyped thresholds and urgency components.
evaluation: Claims C10-C24 describe well-established properties of the CPP and Mu/Beta signals, all supported by extensive citations to prior work. These provide the methodological foundation for using these signals to study accumulation onset timing.

result: Experiment 1 included 21 subjects (after exclusions) for behavioral analysis and 19 for EEG analysis. Experiment 2 included 19 subjects.
evaluation: Claims C33-C35 and C82 provide straightforward methodological details about sample sizes and exclusions, which are clearly stated and appropriate for EEG studies of this type.

result: In Experiment 1, foreperiod duration significantly affected RT, accuracy, missed responses, premature responses, and points earned. Longer foreperiods resulted in faster but less accurate responses with more premature responses, while shorter foreperiods led to slower responses with more misses. Performance peaked at intermediate (1200 ms) foreperiods.
evaluation: Claims C36-C43 report highly significant main effects of foreperiod (all p < 0.001) with appropriate statistical tests and post-hoc comparisons. The pattern of results is internally consistent and supported by the data shown in Figure 1.

result: Conditional accuracy functions revealed that on long foreperiod trials, accuracy was at chance for the fastest responses (closest to evidence onset), suggesting these responses were based on little or no valid sensory evidence. Beyond 2400 ms, accuracy decreased monotonically with RT across all foreperiods.
evaluation: Claims C44-C46 describe patterns in conditional accuracy functions shown in Figure 1d. The interpretation that chance-level accuracy reflects lack of valid evidence (C45) is a reasonable inference from the data pattern.

result: SSVEP analysis showed that sensory evidence representation was stable across foreperiod durations. Target SSVEP increased and non-target SSVEP decreased after the contrast change, but foreperiod duration did not affect SSVEP SNR.
evaluation: Claims C47-C55 report SSVEP results with appropriate statistics (C51-C54 show non-significant effects of foreperiod). This establishes that behavioral differences across foreperiods cannot be attributed to differences in sensory evidence quality, which is critical for the main interpretation.

result: On longer foreperiod trials in Experiment 1, significant CPP build-up was observed before evidence onset, present from session 1 and not varying across training. Pre-evidence CPP amplitude was larger on longer foreperiods and inversely related to RT, with greater pre-evidence build-up associated with faster responses.
evaluation: Claims C56-C62 report the key neural evidence for premature accumulation with strong statistical support (C56: p < 0.002 for 1200ms and p < 0.00002 for 1600ms; C59: p < 0.00002; C60: p < 0.00003). The finding that this was present from session 1 (C57) rules out a learning artifact.

result: Subjects showed a systematic bias toward left choices in premature and fast responses, attributed to the difference in flicker frequency between left (20 Hz) and right (25 Hz) gratings, which affects perceived brightness and contrast.
evaluation: Claims C63-C65 report significant choice biases with strong statistics. The attribution to flicker frequency differences (C66-C67) is supported by citations to psychophysical literature and provides a plausible mechanistic explanation.

result: Mu/Beta lateralisation analysis showed significant pre-evidence motor preparation on longer foreperiod trials, with greater lateralisation on longer foreperiods that scaled inversely with RT. The rate of Mu/Beta lateralisation during the foreperiod also predicted RT.
evaluation: Claims C68-C72 report motor preparation findings parallel to the CPP results, with appropriate statistics (C68: p ≤ 0.002; C69: p = 0.04; C70: p = 0.017; C72: p = 0.006). This provides converging evidence for premature decision formation from a different neural signal.

result: Pre-response CPP and contralateral Mu/Beta amplitudes did not vary with foreperiod duration or RT, consistent with time-invariant decision and motor thresholds. Ipsilateral Mu/Beta was more desynchronized on slower trials, and Mu/Beta lateralisation was stronger on faster trials.
evaluation: Claims C73-C78 report null effects for CPP and contralateral Mu/Beta (appropriate for testing threshold invariance) and significant effects for ipsilateral signals. The pattern is consistent with prior work and the theoretical framework.

result: Summary of Experiment 1: Subjects were unable to align decision formation onset to evidence onset under temporal uncertainty. On longer foreperiod trials, decision formation commenced prematurely, reflected in CPP build-up and Mu/Beta lateralisation, resulting in more false alarms and fast errors.
evaluation: Claims C79-C81 provide an accurate summary of the key findings from Experiment 1, integrating behavioral and neural evidence. The conclusions are well-supported by the preceding claims.

result: Experiment 2 replicated the behavioral findings from Experiment 1, showing significant effects of foreperiod on RT, accuracy, miss rate, premature response rate, and points earned.
evaluation: Claims C83-C87 report highly significant effects (all p ≤ 0.005) that replicate the pattern from Experiment 1, strengthening the generalizability of the findings across different task paradigms.

result: Experiment 2 replicated the neural findings, showing significant pre-evidence CPP build-up and Mu/Beta lateralisation on longer foreperiod trials, with larger CPP amplitudes at evidence onset for longer foreperiods.
evaluation: Claims C88-C91 report replication of the key neural findings with appropriate statistics (C88: p ≤ 0.03; C89: p = 0.009; C90: p = 0.005; C91: p = 0.04), confirming premature accumulation in a different task context.

result: In Experiment 2, pre-response CPP and contralateral Mu/Beta amplitudes did not vary with foreperiod duration or RT, replicating the threshold invariance findings from Experiment 1.
evaluation: Claims C92-C95 report null effects consistent with Experiment 1, with appropriate non-significant statistics (all p > 0.48). This replication strengthens confidence in the threshold invariance interpretation.

result: Motion energy analysis in Experiment 2 showed that fast responses were associated with sustained motion energy favoring the chosen response during the foreperiod. Pre-evidence CPP build-up was significant only when cumulative motion energy consistently favored a particular choice, demonstrating that premature accumulation reflected sensory noise.
evaluation: Claims C96-C100 provide critical evidence that premature accumulation reflects actual sensory noise rather than other processes. The statistics are appropriate (C96: p = 0.04; C98: p = 0.005; C99: non-significant; C100: p = 0.03 for amplitude), though the slope comparison (p = 0.07) is marginal.

result: Sequential foreperiod effects showed that performance on the current trial was modulated by the previous trial's foreperiod. Responses were faster when the previous foreperiod was shorter, and accuracy was higher when foreperiod durations were congruent across consecutive trials. Miss rates on short foreperiods and premature responses on long foreperiods were reduced when foreperiods repeated.
evaluation: Claims C101-C106 report highly significant sequential effects (C101: p < 10^-19; C103: p < 10^-9; C105: p < 10^-10; C106: p = 0.001) demonstrating trial-by-trial adaptation of accumulation onset timing based on recent experience.

result: Neural analysis of sequential effects showed that CPP amplitude at evidence onset was higher when the previous foreperiod was shorter. The absence of slope effects suggests differences arose from accumulation onset timing rather than rate. These findings indicate that decision onset timing is modulated by recent temporal experience.
evaluation: Claims C107-C109 provide the neural mechanism for sequential behavioral effects with appropriate statistics (C107: p = 0.02). The inference about onset vs. rate (C108) is reasonable given the pattern of results, though additional analyses could strengthen this conclusion.

result: When evidence onsets are difficult to discern, participants initiate accumulation endogenously before evidence appears. They adapt accumulation onset timing strategically based on task temporal structure and recent experience, timing onset to approximately coincide with the earliest possible evidence presentation (800 ms), leading to peak performance at intermediate foreperiods.
evaluation: Claims C110-C114 provide well-supported summary interpretations of the main findings. C115 is explicitly speculative about a Bayesian 'regression to the mean' mechanism, which is appropriately qualified and supported by relevant citations.

result: Accumulation onset timing is calibrated based on recent trial foreperiods, with shorter foreperiods leading to earlier onset on subsequent trials. These trial-by-trial adjustments may reflect continuous updating of temporal expectations through monitoring local statistical patterns.
evaluation: Claims C116-C117 summarize the sequential effects findings. C116 is directly supported by the data, while C117 provides a theoretical interpretation supported by citations to normative theories of temporal prediction.

result: Early CPP build-up in Experiment 2 was driven by random fluctuations in motion energy, demonstrating that premature accumulation reflects sensory noise.
evaluation: Claim C118 is directly supported by the motion energy analysis (C96-C100), which showed that CPP build-up tracked random motion fluctuations during the foreperiod.

result: The sequential foreperiod effect observed in this study can be attributed to adjustments in evidence accumulation onset timing.
evaluation: Claim C119 provides a mechanistic explanation for a well-known behavioral phenomenon, supported by the neural evidence showing that CPP onset timing varies with previous trial foreperiod (C107-C109).

result: Neural decision signals (CPP) can be leveraged to directly infer accumulation onset timing, providing insights difficult to obtain from behavior alone.
evaluation: Claims C120-C121 highlight a methodological contribution of the study. The CPP data clearly show pre-evidence accumulation that would be difficult to infer from behavioral measures alone, demonstrating the value of this approach.

result: Main conclusions: (1) Without precise foreknowledge of subtle sensory change timing, observers cannot accurately time accumulation onset, leading to premature responses/fast errors or delayed responses/misses. (2) Accumulation onset timing is controlled by top-down processes, not solely sensory-driven mechanisms. (3) Observers rely on and continuously update representations of task temporal structure.
evaluation: Claims C122-C124 provide accurate high-level summaries of the main findings, well-supported by the convergent behavioral and neural evidence from both experiments.

result: Overall summary of main findings: Subjects systematically initiated evidence accumulation before evidence onset when timing was uncertain, reflected in CPP build-up (which tracked motion energy in Experiment 2) and Mu/Beta lateralisation. This premature accumulation accounted for foreperiod effects on behavior (misses on short trials, premature responses/fast errors on long trials). Accumulation onset timing varied with recent trial history, creating congruency effects on accuracy.
evaluation: Claims C25-C32 provide an integrated summary of the core findings. All are well-supported by the detailed results from both experiments, with strong convergent evidence from behavioral, CPP, Mu/Beta, and motion energy analyses.
